title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: say it after me: a song passed from one mouth to another, no page in sight. Tradition says the Rig Veda was heard, then carried by voice

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: knowledge in verses of praise, opening with Agni, the fire, asked to be easy to reach. Did a lamp or a stove remind you of it? Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

Say it after me. A grandmother sits on the edge of a bed and sings one line of an old song. The child sings it back, a little off. She sings it again, slower. The child tries again, and this time it lands. Next line. Nobody opens a book. There's no screen, no lyrics sheet. The song moves from one mouth into one ear, and lives there now. Years later that child might sing it to someone else, the same way, line by line. A song can cross a lifetime like that without ever touching paper. Hindu tradition says the Rig Veda traveled exactly this way, and it gives the hymns a name for it.
screen: `SAY IT AFTER ME.` → `NO BOOK, NO PAGE.` → `MOUTH TO EAR.`

segments.voice: The Vedas are called shruti, what is heard. Tradition says the hymns weren't invented the way a song is written today. They were seen and heard by rishis, seers, in a kind of deep listening, and then passed on by mouth, teacher to student. Tradition remembers each hymn together with its seer, its god and its meter, so a chanter knows whose hymn this is and how it should sound. Some schools of interpretation, Mimamsa among them, go further: they hold that the Veda has no human author at all. The seers didn't make it. They received it. And yet the hymns sometimes talk about themselves in another way. In one hymn to Agni, the poet says, in paraphrase: I have fashioned this praise for you, as a skilled maker builds a chariot. Fitted, shaped, joined. So the tradition holds two pictures side by side. The hymn is heard, and the hymn is also crafted with care. Some teachers in the tradition hold the two together: a seer can receive something and still work hard to say it well. Which is why the sound matters so much. Vedic chanters learn the words not only straight through but also in patterns that repeat and weave them, so a slip would be caught. The meaning matters. But in this tradition, the sound itself is also part of what's handed on.
screen: `SHRUTI: WHAT IS HEARD.` · `SEEN BY RISHIS, PASSED BY MOUTH.` · `CRAFTED LIKE A CHARIOT.` · `THE SOUND IS PART OF THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen the way a student listens. Sit, and close your eyes. Let the breath settle. Now listen to the room. The near sounds first, then the far ones. Don't name them or judge them. Just receive them, the way a seer is said to receive a hymn. If a song or a line someone once taught you by heart comes to mind, let it play quietly inside, and notice whose voice it's in. If you pray, you can thank the people who carried words to you. The bell holds the time.
What the Rig Veda is. Shruti, what is heard: hymns tradition says were seen by rishis and carried by voice, while one poet calls his hymn something fashioned like a chariot. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Today, teach someone one thing by voice alone: a line, a recipe, a song. Say it, and let them say it back. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Vedic recitation is traditionally learned by ear from a teacher, the student repeating each phrase back, and chanters also learn recitation patterns that repeat and interweave the words to keep the sound exact.

fork.setup: you're a student of Vedic chant. your teacher has just chanted a line. what do you do next?
options: write it down so you won't forget.
say it back, sound for sound.
ask what it means before going on.
fork.reveal: tradition teaches by ear: the student repeats the line back, sound for sound, and the meaning is studied too.

original.note: Sanskrit: a seer. Tradition says the rishis saw and heard the Vedic hymns.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Rig Veda was written by an author at a desk.
what it means: tradition calls it shruti, heard by seers and carried mouth to ear.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 5.2.11, the poet who fashioned a hymn like a chariot, set beside the Mimamsa teaching that the Veda is authorless.

notes: Rig Veda 5.2.11 paraphrased (the chariot-maker image, atakṣam). Confirm the verse number and the paraphrase.

'Tradition remembers each hymn with its seer, its god and its meter' refers to the Anukramani indexes; stated as tradition. Confirm.
